title: One-step KLR simple restriction, induction, and the first-dot index
statement: Let k be any field and R(Q) the graded KLR algebra for a real symmetrizable Cartan datum and any homogeneous Q satisfying the standing symmetry and nonzero extremal-coefficient conditions. Graded simple modules are compared up to internal shift. For a simple S of root weight beta and r=epsilon_i(S)>0, its ordinary one-step last-i restriction has a single simple graded socle and a single simple graded head, each once and of the same shift orbit, with epsilon_i=r-1; its maximum-epsilon composition part has coefficient a grading shift of [r]_i. The last-dot nilpotence index on that restriction is exactly r. The first-end statements hold with epsilon_i^L and the first dot. For every n>=1, Ind(S boxtimes L(i^n)) has a unique simple graded head f_i^n S, occurring once in its whole composition series, with epsilon_i=r+n (also when r=0); all other constituents have smaller epsilon_i. One-step simple socle and simple induction head are partial inverses. A simple S survives the first-strand cyclotomic quotient with exponents lambda_i exactly when epsilon_i^L(S)<=lambda_i for all i. Right restriction preserves surviving simples, while projected right induction has the same simple head when that generic head survives and is zero otherwise. These are shift-orbit assertions and do not assert factorial socle multiplicity.
strategy:
## Nil-Hecke branching computation

Let L_r be the nil-Hecke simple, modeled by the coinvariant algebra C_r=k[t_1,...,t_r]/(e_1,...,e_r) with polynomial multiplication and divided differences. Put z=t_r, and write E_a for elementary symmetric polynomials in t_1,...,t_(r-1). The equations e_a=E_a+z E_(a-1)=0 give E_a=(-z)^a for 1<=a<=r-1, and the final equation gives z^r=0. Consequently

    C_r = k[t_1,...,t_(r-1)] tensor_(k[E_1,...,E_(r-1)]) k[z]/(z^r),

where E_a acts on the second factor by (-z)^a. This is an equality of presented algebras, not a dimension heuristic. The polynomial representation of NH_(r-1) is a free module of rank (r-1)! over its symmetric center and identifies NH_(r-1) with the full matrix algebra over that center. After this specialization its image on C_r is Mat_((r-1)!)(k[z]/(z^r)), and C_r is its standard column module. Thus its graded socle and head are each one shifted L_(r-1), its simple composition coefficient is a shifted [r]_i, and multiplication by z has nilpotence index exactly r. The simple socle is the column over z^(r-1)k, the head the column modulo z. For r=1 this is the statement C_1=k and z=0. The same calculation with the first variable distinguished gives first-end branching. Matrix units and a monic Artin polynomial basis make the computation valid in all characteristics.

The induction NH_r tensor NH_n -> NH_(r+n) of L_r tensor L_n is L_(r+n), up to shift. Every positive full symmetric polynomial acts by zero, since its coproduct is a sum of products of block symmetric polynomials with at least one positive factor. Hence the induced module is a module over the full nil-Hecke central matrix quotient. PBW freeness computes its dimension as binomial(r+n,r)r!n!=(r+n)!, exactly the standard column dimension; it is therefore one simple column, not a factorial number of simples.

## Restriction has a simple socle

Let S have epsilon_i(S)=r>0. The maximum possible epsilon_i of a composition factor of e_i S is r-1 by the exact defining corners. Let U be any simple subobject of e_i S, and put t=epsilon_i(U). The final dot z commutes with R(beta-alpha_i) and acts nilpotently on e_i S: this holds on the whole S by positive dot degree and finite grading support. It preserves the socle and its ungraded isotypic components. On the isotypic component containing U, a suitable nonzero power image has a nonzero kernel copy of the same underlying simple type, killed by z. Absolute simplicity and the finite graded semisimple decomposition let one choose that copy homogeneously, with the appropriate shift. The induction–restriction adjunction therefore gives a nonzero map Ind(U,L_1)->S, hence a surjection. The graded shuffle formula bounds every induced tail by t+1, so r<=t+1. The preceding upper bound gives t=r-1.

Now apply the maximal (r-1)-tail corner p to e_i S, retaining R(beta-r alpha_i) tensor NH_(r-1). Original10 gives Delta_i^r S=N tensor L_r, with epsilon_i(N)=0. Hence

    p(e_i S)=N tensor Res_(NH_(r-1))L_r.

The right side has a single simple socle by the nil-Hecke computation and the absolute simplicity of N. Every simple subobject U of e_i S has t=r-1, so original10 makes pU a nonzero simple object. Exactness of p makes p(soc e_i S) semisimple and injects it into the one-simple socle of p(e_i S). Thus soc e_i S is itself a single simple object, once, with epsilon r-1. This also proves detection: any nonzero submodule of e_i S contains a simple graded submodule U, whose pU is nonzero.

## Simple head and global dot index

Finite graded psi-duality D is exact, takes simples to simples, fixes the corner idempotents and commutes with restriction; it needs no self-dual representative. Apply the socle proof to DS, whose epsilon equals r, and dualize. It follows that e_i S has a single simple head, once. The maximum-tail restriction of the head and socle have the same first factor N up to the corresponding duals and grading shifts: the nil-Hecke head/socle differ only by shift. Original10's unique-head recursion therefore identifies their shift orbits.

On p(e_i S), z^r=0 while z^(r-1)!=0 by the explicit nil-Hecke model. The image of z^r on all of e_i S is a graded submodule. Its p-corner is zero; the just-proved detection property forces that image to be zero. Nonvanishing of z^(r-1) in the p-corner implies its nonvanishing globally. Therefore the last-dot nilpotence index on e_i S is exactly r. Repeating the proof for the first-end maximal restriction gives first-dot nilpotence index exactly epsilon_i^L(S). Notice that this argument uses detection of all submodules; knowing the index only on the maximal corner would not suffice on its own.

## Nonreduced induction and partial inverses

Put M_n=Ind(S,L_n), n>=1. Its maximum tail is at most r+n by shuffle. At tail r+n the Mackey filtration can only retain all n added i-strands and precisely r original terminal i-strands: taking fewer added strands would require more than r from S, while taking fewer original strands would not fill the requested tail. Thus the maximum corner is

    Delta_i^(r+n)M_n = N tensor Ind_(NH_r tensor NH_n)^(NH_(r+n))(L_r tensor L_n)
                      = N tensor L_(r+n),

up to the fixed grading shift. This is one actual surviving filtration term and is simple.

Every simple quotient T of M_n has that maximum tail. Indeed adjunction gives a nonzero injection S tensor L_n -> Delta_i^n T. Restrict its first factor to S's maximal r-tail; the resulting nonzero corner implies epsilon_i(T)>=r+n. The shuffle bound gives equality. The finite semisimple head of M_n therefore has only constituents detected by its simple maximum corner; exactness implies that head is one simple constituent, once. Its maximum corner is the displayed simple module. The kernel of M_n->hd M_n has zero maximum corner, so every other composition factor has smaller epsilon and the head occurs once in the entire composition series.

For n=1 write f_i S=hd M_1 and e-tilde_i T=soc e_i T. Adjunction realizes S in e_i(f_i S), so the simple-socle result gives e-tilde_i f_i S=S, with shifts restored. Conversely if S=soc e_i T, adjunction gives T as a simple quotient of Ind(S,L_1), hence T=f_i S. These are actual partial inverses. The raising operator decreases epsilon by1; lowering increases it by1. Iterating partial inverses shows hd Ind(S,L_n)=f_i^n S: strip the maximum-tail head n times using the unique original10 recursion, or apply the same adjunction and uniqueness at each one-strand stage. All statements hold at the first end by the identical first-end Mackey and dot arguments.

## Exact cyclotomic criterion

Let J^Lambda be generated by x_1^lambda_i on every word beginning with i. It annihilates a simple S exactly when each first-i corner has first-dot index at most lambda_i. The preceding theorem proves that index is epsilon_i^L(S). Thus

    J^Lambda S=0 iff epsilon_i^L(S)<=lambda_i for every i.

If a generator is nonzero, simplicity makes J^Lambda S=S and the quotient projection vanishes. If every generator vanishes, projection is S. This proves the criterion over all fields and Q without citing the omitted proof of LV Proposition2.4. Since first strands are preserved by right restriction, raising preserves the cyclotomic subcategory. For right induction, its generic unique head either survives, in which case quotient induction has that same unique head, or dies, in which case the quotient induction is zero: any nonzero finite module has a simple quotient, and any such quotient of the original induction must be its unique head.

The maximal-epsilon composition factors of e_i S are precisely the same simple shift orbit as its head/socle: their maximal corner is a constituent of N tensor Res L_r, whose single simple type identifies them by the maximal-tail recursion. The nil-Hecke branching calculation gives their graded coefficient as a shift of [r]_i. This concerns the full composition part; the socle and head each have one copy. The proof uses no choice and no self-dual representative.

references.title: Lauda and Vazirani, Crystals from categorified quantum groups, arXiv:0909.1810v2
references.locator: Actually read §2.5/§2.5.1 PDF17–18 and §2.6 Proposition2.4 PDF20; the omitted dot-index/first-strand proof and nonreduced head arguments are supplied locally by nil-Hecke matrix branching and exact maximal-corner detection.

axiom_use: None: explicit finite nil-Hecke matrix units, finite graded duality, exact corners and finite composition series; no self-dual representative or global-basis hypothesis is used.

title: The KLR two-color jump formula and strict elementary embeddings
statement: Let k be any field and R(Q) the graded KLR algebra for a real symmetrizable Cartan datum and any homogeneous Q satisfying the standing symmetry and nonzero extremal-coefficient conditions. Graded simple modules are compared up to internal shift. Set c_i(S)=epsilon_i^L(S) and J_i(S)=max{n>=0:c_i(f_i^n S)=c_i(S)}. This maximum is finite and J_i(S)=epsilon_i(S)+c_i(S)-<h_i,beta>. For i!=j one has c_i(f_j S)=c_i(S); for j=i it stays constant or increases by1, and increase is equivalent to f_i S=f_i^L S and to simplicity of Ind(S,L(i)). Once it increases, it increases at every later right-i step. Put wt(S)=-beta and phi_i=epsilon_i+<h_i,wt>. The maps Psi_i(S)=(e_i^L)^c_i(S) S tensor b_i(-c_i(S)) are strict injective elementary-crystal maps, and every nonvacuum simple has positive extraction at some i. The simple graph is lowering-generated with every generic f_i nonzero. In any first-strand cyclotomic quotient containing S the actual surviving lowering length is lambda_i+epsilon_i(S)-<h_i,beta>. All containing-weight arguments take place in the auxiliary primitive-coroot finite-support datum, leaving R,A,D,Q unchanged, so no positive-dominant-label assumption on the original P is added. Linear divided restriction/G_0 operators satisfy the quantum Serre relation; the simple-socle crystal operators are not asserted to satisfy a linear Serre identity.
strategy:
Use the simple-socle/head symbols e_i,f_i only for crystal operators. Use mathsf E_i^(r) below for exact divided restriction functors and their A-linear G_0 operators. Consume the existing native10 positive second-adjunction contract Coind_(beta,gamma)(M,N)=Ind_(gamma,beta)(N,M){+(beta|gamma)}; all head/socle comparisons in this proof are shift-orbit statements.

For every finite containing-weight argument, first restrict to the finite color support of the modules and the selected i/j strings and use lem-finite-support-regularization-of-quantum-label-weight-modules. Its auxiliary primitive coroots admit labels with independently prescribed nonnegative lambda_l. The KLR algebras and their module, shuffle, restriction and induction calculations are unchanged because A,D,Q are unchanged; the first-strand quotient depends only on these lambda_l integers. Lambda/Omega used below are such auxiliary labels. No existence of a strictly positive dominant weight in the original P is assumed. Transport actual label weights back through the injective finite-support labeling when a label statement is needed. All choices of bounds and coordinates are finite.

## Two elementary tools

For an exact induction functor Ind(A,-), a composition-series argument produces a surjection Ind(A,U)->T from some simple composition factor U of H whenever Ind(A,H)->T is surjective and T simple. Indeed choose the first term in a composition series whose induced image is nonzero; that image is T and the previous term maps to zero. When only one simple factor has the required tail support, it must be this U. This argument obtains an actual map from the simple subquotient; it does not assert that every original map factors through an arbitrarily chosen head.

If epsilon_i(A)=0 and Ind(A,U)->T is nonzero with U,T simple, then epsilon_i(T)=epsilon_i(U). Shuffle gives the upper bound; adjunction injects A tensor U into restriction of T, whose terminal epsilon_i(U) corner is nonzero, giving the lower bound. Consequently every simple factor with the wrong epsilon is excluded in the preceding composition-series argument.

## The jump lemma

Adjunction for Ind(M,L(j))->f_j M and shuffle give

    c_i(M)<=c_i(f_j M)<=c_i(M)+delta_ij.

For i!=j this is equality, and first-end symmetry gives epsilon_i(f_j^L M)=epsilon_i(M). Suppose c_i(f_i M)=c_i(M)+1. Reversed induction Ind(L(i),M) has the same ungraded character as Ind(M,L(i)); character injectivity gives the same ungraded composition factors. Its unique maximal-first-tail factor is f_i^L M, once, so f_i M=f_i^L M. Conversely this equality immediately forces the increase of c_i.

C1, finite psi-duality and the coincidence of one-step head/socle shift orbits give D e_i M=e_i DM and D f_i M=f_i DM on shift orbits. Therefore coInd(M,L_n) has simple socle f_i^n M; the existing positive-shift Coind formula gives soc Ind(M,L_n)=(f_i^L)^n M and soc Ind(L_n,M)=f_i^n M on shift orbits (the actual socle shifts are the coinduction socle shifts minus (root(M),n alpha_i)). If f_i M=f_i^L M, the same simple is both head and socle of Ind(M,L_1), and occurs once in its whole composition series by C1. Such a finite-length module is simple: if its length were greater than1, its simple socle lies in its radical and gives a second occurrence of the head. Ind(M,L_1) is thus simple and equals Ind(L_1,M). Iterated induction and nil-Hecke induction identify Ind(M,L_n)=Ind(L_n,M), up to shift; their unique heads and socles agree and occur once, so they too are simple. In particular c_i(f_i^n M)=c_i(M)+n for all n. Thus once c_i increases, it increases at every later step.

Set J_i(M)=max{n:c_i(f_i^n M)=c_i(M)}. Its finiteness is proved by the separate root-height induction below, using eventual two-color growth and the annihilation lemma, without presuming integrability in an unbounded i-direction. Once finite, the zero-jump lemma proves J_i(f_i M)=max(0,J_i(M)-1); the symmetric jump formula below gives its first-end analogue.

For any Lambda containing M, write p_i^Lambda(M) for its actual surviving f_i length. Once finiteness is established, the first-color criterion and cross-color invariance give exactly

    p_i^Lambda(M)=J_i(M)+lambda_i-c_i(M).                 (1)

Hence differences of p_i for two surviving simples are independent of the containing dominant weight. There is no assumption here that p_i already equals epsilon_i+weight.

## Complete two-color classification

Here is the algebra calculation needed to use the direct §6.3.1 route for general Q, rather than the unproved p5 extension sentence. Fix i!=j, a=-a_ij and t the nonzero coefficient of u^a in Q_ij. The one-j simple has its dot acting by0. Homogeneity gives Q_ij(u,0)=t u^a. For a triple i,j,i whose j-dot acts by0, the divided braid polynomial is, up to the fixed presentation sign,

    t sum_(r=0)^(a-1) x_left^r x_right^(a-1-r).

Mixed Q monomials with positive j-exponent vanish. The coefficient t remains invertible over every field. In the nil-Hecke simple of m strands each dot has nilpotence index exactly m: the coinvariant algebra model k[x_1,...,x_m]/(positive symmetric polynomials) has x_s^m=0 and x_s^(m-1)!=0; the latter follows from the monic Artin basis after permuting s to the chosen last coordinate. Its polynomial representation contains a vector on which this power is nonzero.

For m+n<=a, the length-decreasing quadratic terms at either i/j boundary vanish, since x_i^a=0 on a block of size m or n. The divided braid term vanishes since every r has r>=m or a-1-r>=n. Thus the positive-shuffle span in Ind(L(i^m),L(j),L(i^n)) is invariant under dots, idempotents and crossings: dot slides keep j in the same position; far moves preserve positive length; only the boundary square and i,j,i divided braid can remove the last unequal crossing, and their correction terms just vanished. The quotient supported on i^m j i^n is precisely the simple tensor of the two nil-Hecke simples and L(j), hence is simple, with character [m]!_i[n]!_i i^m j i^n. Any simple of ci+j has a nonzero such corner; a simple submodule in that corner induces onto it, so these exhaust the simples for c<=a. The tensor quotient is generated by its defining corner, giving the indicated quotient map. This constructs the small two-color simples without Serre minimality or Gabber–Kac imports.

For m+n=a+1 with m,n>0, the same divided braid polynomial has a single possibly nonzero term on a tensor of top-dot vectors: r=m-1, a-1-r=n-1. Its coefficient is the unit t. Both neighboring unequal crossings belong to the kernel of a hypothetical quotient supported only at i^m j i^n, so the braid difference would belong to that kernel; its correction instead equals t times a nonzero defining-corner vector generating the tensor simple. This forces the whole induced module into the kernel and contradicts its being proper. For m=0 or n=0 the boundary square replaces the braid: t x_i^a acts nontrivially on the block of a+1 strands. Consequently at the critical degree the induction head cannot remain on a single word. The C1 nonreduced head/once theorem and the linear projective-Serre proof below establish the remaining critical and larger-degree structure.

For c<=a the following direct generic-Q calculation constructs the simple L(i^(c-n) j i^n), 0<=n<=c, with character [c-n]!_i[n]!_i i^(c-n)j i^n and epsilon_i=n, c_i=c-n. These exhaust simples: every simple has a nonzero word corner of this form, that corner has a simple submodule for the tensor product of its three block algebras, and induction from that tensor maps onto the simple. The constructed simple quotient has the only defining-word tensor multiplicity and the unique-head recursion selects it. For uniqueness with a specified n>0 strip one last i and induct on c using C1. For n=0 use first-end stripping; the last and first zero conditions cannot both hold at a positive i-count. Thus there is exactly one simple per n.

Write L(n)=L(i^(a-n) j i^n), 0<=n<=a. To prove Ind(L(n),L_1) simple, C1 gives its head T and epsilon_i(T)=n+1. Shuffle permits only two positions of j in its character: i^(a-n)j i^(n+1) and i^(a-n+1)j i^n. The first position is nonzero by the maximal-tail formula. Here the simple-socle symbols e_i do NOT satisfy quantum Serre relations. Define the EXACT divided restriction functor mathsf E_i^(r)(X)=HOM_(NH_r)(P_(i,r),Delta_i^r X), retaining the remaining R action; it is exact because the divided projective is projective. Its class gives an A-linear operator on G_0, and repeated one-strand restriction has [r]_i! times that class with the native shifts. Native10 projective Serre and induction–restriction adjunction imply sum_(s=0)^(a+1)(-1)^s mathsf E_i^(a+1-s) mathsf E_j^(1) mathsf E_i^(s)=0 on G_0: pair with any projective P of the remaining root weight; the result is the Hom pairing of Ind(P, sum_s(-1)^s P_(i,a+1-s)P_(j,1)P_(i,s)) with X, which vanishes by the native relation; the unscaled perfect cover–simple pairing forces the operator relation. Its sign agrees with native (-1)^(a+1-s) after multiplication by one common sign. Apply THIS LINEAR relation to [T]. Equivalently at the critical full root weight, apply the Hom functional h(-,T) to the projective Serre class. Only the actual word corners i^(a+1-s) j i^s for s=n and s=n+1 can be nonzero, by the preceding two-position shuffle support. The s=n+1 corner is nonzero by epsilon_i(T)=n+1 and the maximal-tail theorem. Applying the divided block idempotents does not erase a nonzero such corner: each nil-Hecke divided idempotent is full, so its tensor product is full in the block algebra and detects every nonzero module. Thus the s=n+1 contribution is a nonzero positive Laurent polynomial (a scalar class in G_0(k)); the alternating relation forces the s=n contribution also nonzero. That actual word support forces c_i(T)=a-n+1=c_i(L(n))+1. No nonlinear crystal Serre identity is used. The jump lemma therefore makes Ind(L(n),L_1) simple. It follows for every m that Ind(L(n),L_m)=Ind(L_m,L(n)) is simple. This proof uses a locally proved Serre relation, not a minimality/Gabber–Kac theorem or a parameter-independence claim.

For c>=a, every simple of ci+j is exactly

    Ind(L(n-(c-a)),L_(c-a)),  c-a<=n<=c, epsilon_i=n.     (2)

Induct on c. A simple with epsilon_i=0 would have only the word i^c j, since there is only one j and any other position of j leaves a terminal i. For c>=a+1 multiply the native projective Serre relation on the LEFT by P_(i,c-a-1) and pair with this simple. Every s>0 term has a terminal i^s block and its actual word corner is zero. The s=0 term has the nonzero defining i^c j corner; the tensor product of the divided nil-Hecke idempotents on its consecutive i-blocks is full and therefore detects it. This gives one nonzero positive Laurent polynomial equal to zero, a contradiction. Equivalently these are exact divided restriction/G_0 operators; no simple-socle crystal operator is substituted into a Serre sum. So strip one i by C1, use the inductive formula and the just-proved commuting/simple induction of L(n), and restore it. This proves existence, uniqueness, and all larger-degree characters. In particular the classifications and composition-series selection show that the head of Ind(L(i^b j i^d),L_m) is L(i^b j i^(d+m)) while b+d+m<a; at and beyond the boundary it is Ind(L(a-b),L_(m-a+b+d)).

A useful consequence: if T is a simple quotient of Ind(L(n_1),...,L(n_r),L_m), then

    epsilon_i(T)=m+sum n_t,  c_i(T)=m+sum(a-n_t).         (3)

For the first equality, shuffle bounds the tail above by that value. Split each L(n_t) as the head of Ind(L(i^(a-n_t)j),L_(n_t)), commute its appended i-block past the subsequent L(n_s) using their just-proved simple commuting induction, and obtain a surjection with all m+sum n_t i-strands at the end. Adjunction gives the matching lower bound. Repeat at the first end for the second equality. If Ind(B,L(n))->T is nonzero then epsilon_i(T)=epsilon_i(B)+n by the same stripping/commuting argument.

If B is a nontrivial simple of ci+dj with epsilon_i(B)=0, strip a last j, then strip the newly exposed maximal i-tail b. This gives Ind(B',L_b,L(j))->B with epsilon_i(B')=0. The classification (2) and simple-subquotient selection force b<=a and select L(i^b j). Repeating decreases height, giving

    Ind(L(i^b_1 j),...,L(i^b_r j))->B,  0<=b_t<=a.       (4)

All factors are actual constructed two-color simples.

## Eventual first-tail calculation for two-color modules

Let M be simple of ci+dj, m=epsilon_i(M), and let N=e_i^m M. Choose (4) for N. Induction then gives a surjection

    Ind(L(i^b_1 j),...,L(i^b_r j),L_(m+h))->f_i^h M.

Move the appended i-strands through the factors from right to left. The classification says that a factor L(i^b j) absorbs a-b i-strands to become L(a-b); beyond that point additional i-strands commute past it. Simple-subquotient selection uses epsilon_i of the target to exclude every lower-tail factor. Thus, for m+h>=sum(a-b_t), there is a surjection

    Ind(L(a-b_1),...,L(a-b_r),L_g)->f_i^h M,
    g=m+h-sum(a-b_t).

Equation (3) yields

    c_i(f_i^h M)=h+m-ar+2 sum b_t.                       (5)

This is eventual linear growth of slope1, proving J_i(M)<infinity for two-color M. The absorption algorithm in the insufficient-i case stops at the unique factor s satisfying sum_(t>s)(a-b_t)<=m+h<sum_(t>=s)(a-b_t), with that factor L(i^b_s j i^g') and all factors to its right saturated; the same classification proves that case as well.

Let T=f_j M, i!=j, gamma=epsilon_i(T). The map Ind(N,L_m,L(j))->T and simple-subquotient selection choose the unique simple U_gamma of mi+j with that tail. The classification gives gamma=m-(a-n), 0<=n<=a, and f_i^a U_gamma=Ind(L(n),L_m). For sufficiently large h, absorb the appended i-strands through U_gamma, then through all factors (4). Equation (3) now gives

    c_i(f_i^h T)=h+m-n-ar+2 sum b_t=c_i(f_i^h M)-n.      (6)

All selections are justified by the exact induction, the tail bound when the preceding factor has epsilon_i=0, and the strict lower-tail property of C1. Choose omega_i equal to (5) at some sufficiently large h and other omega_l large enough for M and T; cross-color invariance ensures those other first-tail bounds are unchanged along their f_i strings. Equations (5)–(6), the slope1 continuation, and the cyclotomic criterion give p_i^Omega(M)=h and p_i^Omega(T)=h+n. Equation (1) shows their difference is independent of the containing weight. Thus in any common containing quotient,

    epsilon_i(T)=m-(a-n),  p_i(T)=p_i(M)+n.              (7)

For j=i, C1 and the definition of p_i instead give epsilon_i(f_i M)=m+1 and p_i(f_i M)=p_i(M)-1.

## Annihilation and survival lemmas

Let A survive Lambda and let k=p_i^Lambda(A), assumed finite. If t>k, C1 says Ind(A,L_t) has only one simple quotient f_i^t A, which dies under projection. Therefore its projected module is zero: otherwise that finite-dimensional projection would have a surviving simple quotient, contradicting uniqueness. Appending any further factor U keeps the projection zero. To see this directly, choose tensor generators for A,L_t and U; the first two induced factors lie in their cyclotomic ideal multiple, and that same ideal embeds as a first-strand ideal in the full induction, so their tensors still lie in the full ideal multiple. If B is simple with c_i(B)>k, write B as the head of Ind(L_(c_i(B)),C) using the first-tail lemma. Exact induction and right exact projection now give

    pr_Lambda Ind(A,B)=0.                               (8)

Suppose instead epsilon_i(A)=epsilon_j(A)=0, B is simple of ci+dj, and c_i(B)<=k. Put b=c_i(B), C=(e_i^L)^b B. Ind(A,L_b,C)->Q is surjective for every simple quotient Q of Ind(A,B). In its first two factors the unique head f_i^b A survives. Any other factor U of Ind(A,L_b) has epsilon_i(U)<b. The original defining A|i^b|C corner of Q is nonzero by adjunction. No Ind(U,C) has this defining corner. Every word of A ends in a color outside {i,j}; in any shuffle producing U from Ind(A,L_b), all original A i/j letters occur before A's final outside-color letter, since their order is preserved. In the target defining A|i^b|C word, the prefix through that final outside-color letter contains exactly the original A i/j counts. Thus no j from C can occur in that prefix: it would increase the j count, and no original A j can move past that final letter to compensate. Nor can an added i from C or from the L_b block occur there, by the identical i-count argument. The following i^b block cannot get an i from C, because C has first-i tail0, so every nonempty word of C starts in j; its preceding j can enter neither the prefix just counted nor the pure i^b block. Hence all b consecutive i after the final outside-color letter must come from U, giving a terminal i-tail of length at least b in U, contrary to epsilon_i(U)<b. If C is the vacuum the same conclusion is immediate. This is the actual count/ordering exclusion, rather than an inference from the smaller-epsilon inequality alone. Thus the simple-subquotient selection lemma produces Ind(f_i^b A,C)->Q. Shuffle bounds c_i(Q)<=c_i(f_i^b A)+c_i(C)<=lambda_i. The same argument for j proves survival in the j-coordinate provided c_j(B)<=p_j^Lambda(A). All other coordinates are bounded by c_l(A), since B has only colors i,j. In particular choosing lambda_j sufficiently large ensures that extra inequality: c_j(f_j^d A)<=c_j(A)+d by shuffle, so lambda_j>=c_j(A)+d ensures p_j^Lambda(A)>=d>=c_j(B), without using a normal-length formula.

This survival lemma uses the actual defining-corner exclusion, not merely the inequality epsilon_i(U)<b in isolation; the latter would not control an arbitrary additional factor. It is precisely why A is required to be reduced at both i and j.

## Finiteness of jump for every simple: a separate height induction

This avoids a tacit integrability assumption in the source. The vacuum has f_i^n 1=L_n and c_i(L_n)=n, so J_i(1)=0. Assume finiteness for all strictly smaller heights than M. If r=epsilon_i(M)>0, put N=e_i^r M; then M=f_i^r N. Once first-tail growth has begun it continues at every step, by the jump lemma. Thus J_i(M)=max(0,J_i(N)-r), which is finite by induction.

If epsilon_i(M)=0 and M is nonvacuum, choose a terminal color j with epsilon_j(M)>0; necessarily j!=i. Alternately strip maximal j- and i-tails until both vanish. Height strictly decreases at the first stripping, so the resulting A has smaller height than M. Exact induction reconstructs M as a simple quotient of Ind(A,B), where B is a simple two-color module with epsilon_i(B)=0 and epsilon_i(A)=epsilon_j(A)=0. To choose B, apply the simple-subquotient selection lemma to the induced product of all stripped blocks; the terminal-tail bounds pick an actual simple factor. C1's strict-leading factor selection gives surjections Ind(A,f_i^h B)->f_i^h M for every h. Choose a dominant Lambda containing both A and M. By inductive J_i(A)<infinity, equation (1) gives finite k=p_i^Lambda(A). Equation (5) proves c_i(f_i^h B)>k for all sufficiently large h. Equation (8) forces pr_Lambda f_i^h M=0. If J_i(M) were infinite, cross-color invariance and constant c_i would instead make every f_i^h M survive that same Lambda by the cyclotomic criterion. This contradiction proves finiteness. Now (1) is established for every simple without assuming normality or per-color categorical integrability.

## Transfer of (7) to arbitrary root support

Let M,T=f_j M survive Lambda and i!=j. Strip m=epsilon_i(M) to N, then alternately strip i/j tails from N until obtaining A reduced at both colors. Reconstruct N as a simple quotient of Ind(A,B_0), with B_0 a two-color simple reduced at i. Its j-tail equals that of N by the upper/lower tail bounds. Strict-leading selection converts

    Ind(A,B_0,L_m)->M

into Ind(A,B)->M with B=f_i^m B_0 and epsilon_i(B)=m. Similarly the j-leading selection gives Ind(A,f_j B)->T and epsilon_i(f_j B)=epsilon_i(T). For every h the same argument gives Ind(A,f_i^h B)->f_i^h M and Ind(A,f_i^h f_j B)->f_i^h T.

Choose Omega containing all four A,M,B,f_j B, with omega_j sufficiently large to make the survival lemma's j-condition automatic for every candidate two-color factor above. Its j count is fixed while i-count varies, and cross-color invariance fixes its c_j. Other omega_l can be fixed because two-color factors have no other colors. Put h=p_i^Omega(M), h'=p_i^Omega(T), and k=p_i^Omega(A). These numbers are finite by the preceding height induction. Applying the contrapositive of (8) at the surviving endpoints gives c_i(f_i^h B)<=k and c_i(f_i^h' f_j B)<=k. Applying the contrapositive of the survival lemma at the next, nonsurviving endpoints gives c_i(f_i^(h+1) B)>k and c_i(f_i^(h'+1) f_j B)>k. Since each increase is at most1, both surviving endpoint coordinates equal k. Since an increase has begun, their jumps are zero.

Equation (1) applied to those endpoint modules yields p_i^Omega(f_i^h B)=omega_i-k=p_i^Omega(f_i^h' f_j B). Subtracting gives

    p_i^Omega(f_j B)-p_i^Omega(B)=h'-h
      =p_i^Omega(T)-p_i^Omega(M).

The two-color formula (7) gives its value n, where epsilon_i(T)=m-(a-n), 0<=n<=a. Equation (1) and cross-color invariance make p_i(T)-p_i(M) independent of containing quotient, proving (7) for arbitrary support.

## The jump formula

For every surviving M of root weight beta, prove

    p_i^Lambda(M)=lambda_i+epsilon_i(M)-<h_i,beta>       (9)

by induction on height. At the vacuum, p_i=lambda_i because f_i^n 1=L_n has first-tail n; epsilon=0. At positive height choose a last color j and N=e_j M, so M=f_j N and N survives the same quotient. If j=i, epsilon increases1 and actual lowering length decreases1, while <h_i,beta> increases2; (9) follows. If j!=i, equation (7) gives p_i(M)-p_i(N)=n and epsilon_i(M)-epsilon_i(N)=-(a-n), while <h_i,beta>-<h_i,beta-alpha_j>=-a. Again (9) follows. The proof never uses a connected-normality recognition theorem.

Choose any dominant weight containing a generic simple M. Combine (1) and (9):

    J_i(M)=epsilon_i(M)+c_i(M)-<h_i,beta>.              (10)

The right side is invariant under first/last reversal, so all first-end versions of jump and decrease formulas follow. This completes the actual full-support jump calculation, subject only to the explicitly listed local PBW/Mackey/Serre/coinduction suppliers and C1.

## Strict elementary embeddings: all branch cases

For generic wt(M)=-beta put c=c_i(M), bar M=(e_i^L)^c M, and Psi_i(M)=bar M tensor b_i(-c). Reversal symmetry and (10) show that applying f_i^L decreases jump by1 until it becomes zero. Since c_i(bar M)=0, initially J_i(bar M)=epsilon_i(bar M)+<h_i,wt(bar M)>. While jump is positive, first-end lowering preserves epsilon_i; after jump reaches zero, zero-jump equality makes each first-end lowering equal right lowering and epsilon_i increases1. Therefore

    epsilon_i(M)=max(epsilon_i(bar M),c-<h_i,wt(bar M)>).

For e_i, if epsilon_i(bar M)>=c-<h_i,wt(bar M)>, the jump of (e_i^L)M is positive when c>0. Raising cannot decrease c: otherwise zero-jump applied to e_i M would force e_i M=e_i^L M, contradicting that positive jump. Thus it preserves c, and cross-end stripping identifies the stripped result with e_i bar M. If epsilon_i(bar M)<c-<h_i,wt(bar M)>, then J_i(e_i^L M)=0, so zero-jump gives f_i(e_i^L M)=M and e_i M=e_i^L M; its first-tail is c-1 and stripping gives bar M. At c=0 only the first branch can occur. At epsilon_i(M)=0 the max formula forces epsilon_i(bar M)=0 and phi_i(bar M)>=c, so tensor raising is zero in its first branch. These are exactly the tensor e_i branch inequalities, including equality in the first branch.

For j!=i, first-tail invariance and Mackey stripping give (e_i^L)^c f_j M=f_j bar M, hence the lowering rule directly; applying this to e_j M gives the raising rule whenever it is nonzero. For zero raising, the equality of epsilon_j(M) and epsilon_j(bar M), obtained by repeated first-end lowering invariance, makes both sides zero. Weight is preserved, the max formula preserves epsilon_i, cross-color invariance preserves all other epsilon, and phi=epsilon+weight is consequently preserved. The map is injective because M=(f_i^L)^c bar M. Thus Psi_i is strict. A nonvacuum M has a word beginning with some i, so some c_i(M)>0; every elementary coordinate is nonpositive. Generic lowering generation follows from repeated right-socle stripping, and all f_i are nonzero by C1.

The module crystal now satisfies all finite-extraction comparison hypotheses: lowering generation, everywhere nonzero generic lowering, strict elementary embeddings, nonpositive elementary coordinates, and positive extraction at every nonvacuum vertex. The subsequent canonical extraction lemma supplies the independent canonical comparison crystal; no connected rank-one normality assertion is used here.

For the remaining i-lowering check, f_i is nonzero in the generic module crystal and in the elementary tensor target: either it acts on the everywhere-lowerable first factor or on the elementary string. Applying the already verified raising identity to f_i M gives e_i Psi_i(f_i M)=Psi_i(M). Tensor partial inverses then force Psi_i(f_i M)=f_i Psi_i(M). This proves strict lowering including its opposite equality convention, rather than merely saying its check is similar.

title: Canonical elementary crystal extraction and highest-weight survivors
statement: For every real symmetrizable Cartan datum, the canonical negative-half crystal has strict elementary embeddings Psi_i(b)=bar b tensor b_i(-c_i(b)), where c_i(b)=epsilon_i(star b), bar b=(e_i^star)^c_i(b)b, c_i(bar b)=0, and every nonvacuum vertex has positive extraction for some i. The negative-half reversal star permutes B(infinity) without signs; this unsigned conclusion is proved from the existing signed lattice theorem and positive highest-weight tensor residues, not assumed. The survivors of pi_lambda are exactly c_i(b)<=lambda_i for all i; with weight lambda+wt(b), inherited raising and surviving lowering, and epsilon/phi, they are B(lambda). Any two lowering-generated, everywhere-lowerable negative crystals with strict nonpositive elementary extractions and positive extraction at every nonvacuum vertex are uniquely isomorphic by their lowering words; the proof uses finite color cycles and terminates after a height bound. Consequently for any field and any general homogeneous nondegenerate Q of the first two lemmas, the shift-orbit simple-module crystal is canonically B(infinity), its first-strand cyclotomic simple graph is B(lambda), and the graph labeled by indecomposable projective COVERS P(S) is the same graph under the unscaled cover–simple pairing. Projective crystal operators here mean operators transported on cover labels; no arbitrary #-dual-of-simple identification, generic global-basis theorem, or independent linear Kashiwara action on the projective class basis is asserted.
strategy:
## Right strings and the adapted survivor criterion, initially with signs

Define the right string operators by star conjugating the left normalized Kashiwara operators. Because star is an isometry of the actual crystal lattice and signed crystal set, every positive crystal residue b lies in exactly one right-string position c_i(b)>=0. On a lattice lift u one has

    u=sum_(n>=0) u_n F_i^(n),   u_n in ker(star e_i' star),

with every u_n in the crystal lattice, and modulo q only the component n=c_i(b) is nonzero. Its top coefficient has residue ±bar b for some positive crystal residue bar b with c_i(bar b)=0. For the negative half the lattice-component argument is proved directly by the same finite tail calculation as the module string lemma: if u=sum_n F_i^(n)v_n, set T_n=e-tilde_i^n u; then v_n=T_n-f-tilde_i T_(n+1) lies in the lattice. Induction on the largest position, using the residue partial inverse, shows that a basis residue has exactly one nonzero component and that its top residue is positive. Root height makes the tails finite. This proves the half version without applying an integrable-module-only Statement to U^-. Conjugating this argument through the signed lattice theorem gives the asserted signed right version, without assuming unsigned star. The integer c_i(b) is epsilon_i of the absolute value of star b.

The field right ideal U^- F_i^t is the direct sum of right-string positions n>=t. Its adapted global subset is therefore precisely the positive indices b with c_i(b)>=t: conjugate the already proved left-string adapted global subset through star, whose possible signs do not affect which A-basis vectors span the ideal. The based quotient's field kernel is the sum of these right ideals at t=lambda_i+1. Since all are adapted to ONE global basis, their sum is the span of the union of their basis subsets. Therefore

    pi_lambda(b)!=0 iff c_i(b)<=lambda_i for every i.    (A)

This proves the highest-weight survivor criterion already with signed star. It neither assumes unsigned star nor infers an adapted intersection from an arbitrary linear sum. The surviving residues are bijective with B(lambda) by the existing based quotient/grand loop. Raising cannot turn a survivor into a killed nonzero residue: if e_i b were killed, the ALL-residue lowering identity pi_lambda(f_i(e_i b))=f_i pi_lambda(e_i b)=0 and the negative-half partial inverse f_i e_i b=b would force b killed, a contradiction. Thus every nonzero raising iterate of a survivor survives. Combining this with the surviving-residue raising identity proves equality of the entire raising lengths, epsilon_i(pi_lambda b)=epsilon_i(b), including the zero endpoint. This supplies the precise statistic identification used later in the finite-model construction without circularly using elementary embeddings. Raising on survivors and surviving lowering are exactly these existing projection compatibilities. The shifted statistics are epsilon_i(b) and epsilon_i(b)+<h_i,lambda+wt(b)> because B(lambda) is the actual highest-weight module crystal; raising preservation gives epsilon equality, and its rank-one formula gives phi.

## Canonical elementary embedding by finite highest-weight tensor models

Fix color i and a finite set of lowering words of height at most H. Work in the regularized finite support. Choose lambda_i=0 and lambda_j large for j!=i, large enough that no right ideal for those j meets any relevant root component of height at most H+1. Choose N>H+1. The total label lambda+N Lambda_i is then large at every relevant color, so its projection identifies the canonical B(infinity) vertices and all edges under consideration with the corresponding finite-degree vertices of B(lambda+N Lambda_i). Apply the strict highest-weight tensor embedding into B(lambda) tensor B(N Lambda_i).

Throughout these finite lowering paths the second factor is a pure i-string f_i^m u_(N Lambda_i). Indeed initially it is highest. For j!=i its epsilon_j is0 at every pure i-string position: E_j commutes with F_i and kills the highest vector, so all such vectors are E_j-highest. The first factor's phi_j is positive and larger than any second epsilon_j in the bounded degree, because lambda_j is chosen large. Thus both lowering and raising of any j!=i act on the first factor. Color i preserves the pure i-string form. Its string endpoint N is not reached in this height bound.

Lift the first residue b_1 uniquely to its surviving positive residue b' in B(infinity). Replace the second pure i-position m by b_i(-m) in the elementary crystal. The finite tensor rules become exactly those on B(infinity) tensor B_i: for i, lambda_i=0 means the first phi_i is epsilon_i(b')+<h_i,wt(b')>, and the second epsilon_i is m. For j!=i the elementary statistics are -infinity, so its tensor rule selects the first factor, just as the large-lambda finite model does. The finite tensor epsilon formula reduces to epsilon_j(b') for j!=i because lambda_j is large; for i it reduces to max(epsilon_i(b'),m-<h_i,wt(b')>). Root weights add to wt(b')-m alpha_i. Thus the replacement preserves the generic weight, epsilon and formal phi statistics as well as every considered operator.

This construction is independent of lambda,N WITHOUT assuming a stabilization theorem. Define its candidate value on a lowering word w by computing w(u_infinity tensor b_i(0)) using the actual generic tensor rules. The preceding finite-model argument shows that this computation agrees with the replacement of the finite tensor image for every bounded path. If two words w,w' give the same b in B(infinity), choose one common finite bound and one common pair lambda,N. Their images in B(lambda+N Lambda_i) coincide, hence their strict tensor images coincide, and the unique surviving lifts of their first factors coincide. Therefore the candidate generic tensor values coincide. Conversely if the candidate values coincide, choose the same finite model for the two words; its first-factor projections and second positions coincide, and injectivity of Phi followed by the large-label projection identification gives w u_infinity=w' u_infinity. This proves a well-defined injective Psi_i, independent of all choices.

For lowering use the same finite model on a word and that word with one appended operator. For raising use a model containing the vertex, its raising neighbor if nonzero, and the next boundary; strictness of finite Phi and the already checked branch/statistic formulas give Psi_i(e_j b)=e_j Psi_i(b), including zero. Hence

    Psi_i:B(infinity)->B(infinity) tensor B_i

is strict, sends the vacuum to u_infinity tensor b_i(0), and every elementary coordinate is nonpositive. This is an actual finite-word construction, rather than a citation to Kashiwara Theorem8.2.

## Identifying the elementary coordinate with the right-string index

The remaining coordinate identification can be checked on the coproduct rather than assumed from unsigned star. For a homogeneous P of root beta, the coefficient of one i in the second tensor factor of Delta(P), after extracting its toral K_i, is e_i''(P). On homogeneous root beta this derivative is

    e_i''(P)=q_i^(<h_i,beta>-2) (star e_i' star)(P).

Check this first on a generator. Both sides then satisfy the same twisted deletion rule, with prefix versus suffix twists interchanged; the displayed homogeneous scalar converts one rule into the other. Hence their kernels agree. Coassociativity or repeated deletion shows that every higher pure-second-i coefficient is a nonzero field scalar multiple of the corresponding repeated derivative; it therefore vanishes on P in the right-string kernel. Thus projecting Delta(P) onto the terms with pure i root degree in the second factor leaves exactly P tensor1.

Apply this to the right expansion u=sum_n u_n F_i^(n) above, acting on v_lambda tensor v_(N Lambda_i) with lambda_i=0. Every mixed-color second-factor term has a different second root degree and is removed by the pure-i projection. For u_n in the right kernel only u_n tensor1 survives that projection. In Delta F_i^(n), every term whose first divided power F_i^(a) has a>0 kills v_lambda before u_n acts. The remaining term is K_i^n tensor F_i^(n), and K_i^n v_lambda=v_lambda because lambda_i=0. Therefore the exact pure-second-i projection is

    sum_n pi_lambda(u_n) tensor F_i^(n)v_(N Lambda_i).   (B)

No uncontrolled q shift occurs in this formula with the actual native coproduct. The derivative equality above is only used to identify the kernel; scalar rescalings do not change it.

The coefficient u_c, c=c_i(b), has signed positive crystal residue ±bar b with right index0. Its projection at lambda_i=0 survives by (A); all other coordinates survive because lambda_j is large. Thus its projected residue is nonzero. Every n!=c coefficient has zero crystal residue. Formula (B) consequently has exactly one nonzero pure-i tensor residue, at position c. On the other hand Phi(pi_(lambda+N Lambda_i)b) is a positive pure-i tensor residue by the finite model. It follows that its elementary coordinate m is exactly c_i(b), and that the top right-string coefficient u_c has POSITIVE residue bar b, not negative. Thus

    Psi_i(b)=bar b tensor b_i(-c_i(b)),
    c_i(bar b)=0,  b=(f_i^right)^(c_i(b)) bar b.          (C)

In particular every nonvacuum b has positive extraction at some i: star b is a signed nonvacuum crystal residue, and the canonical lowering-generated crystal has a nonzero raising direction on its absolute value.

## Unsigned star follows rather than being assumed

Induct on root height. The vacuum is fixed by star. For a positive-height b choose i with c_i(b)>0. Formula (C) gives b=(f_i^right)^c bar b with bar b a POSITIVE residue of strictly smaller height. Apply star:

    star b=f_i^c(star bar b).

By induction star bar b is positive, and canonical lowering preserves positive crystal residues. Therefore star b is positive. Since star is an involution, it permutes B(infinity) bijectively without signs. This proves unsigned star for every real symmetrizable datum from the actual signed theorem plus tensor positivity. Then c_i(b)=epsilon_i(star b) is the usual epsilon_i^star, and (C) is the exact canonical elementary extraction formula. The proof does not invoke a symmetric-type geometric basis.

## Identification of the generic and cyclotomic module crystals

the preceding local one-step and jump/embedding lemmas construct the generic module strict elementary embeddings, with extraction coordinate epsilon_i^L and positive extraction on every nonvacuum module. Both its graph and the canonical graph just constructed are generated by lowering words from their vacua and have every lowering operator nonzero. The finite-extraction comparison lemma proved next identifies the two graphs uniquely by lowering words. Strictness also forces their elementary extraction coordinates to agree: the comparison tensor identity holds on the vacuum and on every lowering word, so

    epsilon_i^L(M)=epsilon_i^star(b_M).

The local one-step lemma's first-dot criterion identifies the cyclotomic module vertices with epsilon_i^star(b_M)<=lambda_i. Equation (A) identifies exactly that subset with the surviving canonical vertices, hence with B(lambda). Existing projection compatibility proves the raising and surviving-lowering correspondence, while The local jump lemma's actual normal-length formula gives the canonical epsilon/phi data. This proves the full all-field/general homogeneous-Q simple crystal theorem, using exactly the stated local quantum and algebra suppliers. Projective vertices are labeled by the indecomposable projective COVER P(M) of each simple M. The cover–simple Hom pairing transports this graph: E/F crystal labels on covers mean P(e-tilde M), P(f-tilde M), with zero when the simple label is zero. This does not identify P(M) with an arbitrary # dual of M. Independently defined projective Kashiwara operators still require their exact leading-term convention.

## Finite-extraction comparison proof

There is a smaller recognition contract for this application, whose proof is elementary. Suppose C and D are crystals, each generated from its unique weight-zero vertex by lowering words, every f_i is everywhere nonzero, and each has strict elementary embeddings Psi_i with nonpositive elementary coordinates and a positive coordinate for some i on every nonvacuum vertex. Assume the weight support of a vertex is finite and extraction subtracts a nonnegative multiple of alpha_i from its root weight. Then there is a unique crystal isomorphism C=D carrying the two vacua to each other.

Proof. Fix a finite color set containing the support of a lowering word. Cycle through these colors, applying Psi_i to the current first factor, and leave every elementary tensor factor already extracted in place. Tensoring a strict embedding with identity maps is strict: for each color the tensor max formulas preserve epsilon/phi and weight, hence preserve the branch inequality including equality. Therefore every finite composite is strict and injective. Each extraction lowers the nonnegative height of the first factor by its elementary coordinate c. If an entire cycle makes no extraction from a nonvacuum factor, that factor is unchanged throughout the cycle, yet its support has a color with positive extraction, contradiction. Thus after at most the starting height many cycles (and one harmless final cycle) the first factor is the vacuum. Extraction of absent colors is zero: a nonzero alpha_i extraction would give a residual root weight with negative alpha_i coefficient, forbidden. Consequently this finite procedure works in both crystals using the same finite color cycle.

For a word w of length h, use h+1 cycles. Every prefix has height at most h, so both images of every prefix have vacuum first factor. Strictness computes the image of w by applying that same lowering word to the same tensor of a vacuum and elementary zero vertices. While the underlying vacua belong to different crystals, their weights and epsilon/phi are identical and their raising operators vanish; at each intermediate prefix the first factor is still the vacuum, so a nonzero lowering operation cannot take place in that first factor. All operations occur in the identical elementary factors, and the resulting elementary coordinates are identical. If two words w,w' produce the same vertex in C, use a common finite color set and enough cycles for both lengths; their identical C images give identical coordinate tensors, hence identical D images and, by injectivity, identical D vertices. Interchanging C and D gives the converse. Mapping a lowering word in C to that word in D is therefore a well-defined bijection. It preserves lowering by construction, raising by partial inverses, weights by word content, and epsilon/phi because the common strict finite tensor embeddings preserve these statistics. Uniqueness follows from lowering generation. This proves the lemma.
